props.title: Jules and Jim
props.initialSlug: A love triangle tests friendship in 1900s Paris

sections.content: François Truffaut's masterpiece Jules and Jim (1962) revolutionized the French New Wave with its innovative editing, mobile camera work, and complex exploration of a decades-spanning love triangle. The film's influence echoes through later works like The Dreamers (2003) and Y Tu Mamá También (2001). Truffaut's adaptation of Henri-Pierre Roché's semi-autobiographical novel captures the exuberant spirit of pre-WWI Europe through to the 1930s, with Jeanne Moreau's Catherine emerging as one of cinema's most fascinating characters - free-spirited, unpredictable, and ultimately tragic.

sections.content: The film's technical innovations were groundbreaking for 1962. Raoul Coutard's cinematography employs freeze frames, newsreel footage, and whip pans that would influence directors for generations. This visual playfulness appears in later French classics like The Mother and the Whore (1973) and contemporary works such as The French Dispatch (2021). The movie's fluid approach to time and memory created a template for non-linear storytelling that directors like Alain Resnais would expand upon in Hiroshima Mon Amour (1959).

At its heart, Jules and Jim explores the complexity of love and friendship with remarkable maturity. Unlike Hollywood's treatment of love triangles in films like Design for Living (1933), Truffaut avoids moral judgment. The three-way relationship between Jules, Jim, and Catherine feels authentic and painful rather than sensational. This emotional honesty influenced later explorations of polyamory in films like Sunday Bloody Sunday (1971) and Vicky Cristina Barcelona (2008). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Cinema

sections.content: The film's DNA can be found throughout contemporary cinema. Before Sunrise (1995) echoes its romantic walks through European cities. The Worst Person in the World (2021) channels Catherine's spirit of feminine freedom and complexity. Even Wes Anderson's The Royal Tenenbaums (2001) borrows its literary narrative style and bittersweet tone. The movie's influence extends beyond art house cinema into mainstream works like Inglourious Basterds (2009), which directly references Truffaut's distinctive freeze frames.
